claims.quote: Variants in SYNGAP1 cause a rare childhood-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE).
We identified 185 children with likely pathogenic/pathogenic variants in SYNGAP1; 156 had epilepsy (n = 156/185, 84.3 %).
Limited reports describe palliative surgical procedures such as corpus callosotomy (CC) and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) in SYNGAP1-related DEE.
Limited reports describe palliative surgical procedures such as corpus callosotomy (CC) and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) in SYNGAP1-related DEE.
Eleven children had VNS (n = 11/15, 73.3 %), and the median follow-up was 3.3 years (IQR 5.6, 3.3).
Seven children had an initial > 50 % seizure reduction (n = 7/11, 63.6 %), 2 had worsening (n = 2/11, 18.2 %), 1 had no change (n = 1/11, 9.1 %), and 1 had an unknown response (n = 1/11, 9.1 %).
VNS response was sustained in 3 children (3/11, 27.3 %).
Two children (n = 2/15, 13.3 %) had CC only with a mean follow-up of 3.1 years; 1 became seizure-free, and the other had > 50 % seizure reduction.
One child from our centre had a sustained > 80 % seizure reduction (1.5 years) following CC at 7 years.
CC appeared to be more effective in the few treated.
